sections.COMMENTS:
A more than 1000 km-long contraction belt runs along the eastern margin of the Adriatic Sea from the Alpine domain (to the North) to the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (to the south). The various part of this fold and thrust belt are known, from north to south, as Dinarides, Albanides and Hellenides and result from the continental collision between the European and African plates. The outer portion of these chains is partly located offshore and characterized by a number of thrust fronts that seems to be contemporaneously active.
Albanides and Hellenides domains constitute the southernmost portion of the chain.
In this area the thick continental crust of the Apulia domain enters the deformation zone of the Hellenide chain (Kokinou et al., 2005; Shaw and Jackson, 2010; Royden and Papanikolaou, 2011).
The complex structure of this thrust and fold belt, imaged in several seismic profiles accomplished mostly for hydrocarbon exploration, shows a shallow set of thrust sheets that detach at about 8-10 km on an evaporite layer. At greater depths, seismic lines provides some indications of the presence of reverse faults that reach greater depths.
Local convergence between Apulia and the Hellenide domain seems to be of 5-10 mm/y (Hollenstein et al., 2008).
The available focal mechanisms indicate dominant reverse faulting with SW-NE horizontal P-axes (Papazachos et al., 1999); few strike-slip events are also present but generally have smaller earthquake magnitude (Vannucci et al., 2004; European-Mediterranean RCMT catalog, Pondrelli et al., 2006; 2007; 2011).
This area is characterized by diffuse seismicity with occasional M>6 events. The largest earthquakes of this area occurred in 1278, 1732 and 1786 near Kerkira Island with estimated magnitudes of about 6.5-6.6 (SHEEC; Stucchi et al., 2012). Another earthquake of estimeted magnitude of 6.7 occurred in northern Albania, near Durres, in 1270 (SHEEC; Stucchi et al., 2012). The largest earthquake of the instrumental era occurred on 29 June 2007 SE of Kerkira Island with a magnitude of 5.6 (EMEC; GrÃ¼nthal and WahlstrÃ¶m, 2012).
We propose that this Source is on the most external thrust fault that characterize the Hellenide chain along the Greek coast.
Average strike and rake computed by Papazachos et al. (1999) from focal mechanisms are consistent with plate motion vectors derived from GPS data and the orientation of the thrust front reported by many authors. We inferred dip from focal mechanisms (Global CMT catalogue) and from the average dip of the thrust faults detected on seismic profiles.
Slip rates are partitioned among the faults to account for the local convergence.
